A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NeoBERT. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: V1 reports original GLUE ablations, contrastive fine-tuning evaluations on MTEB, Wikipedia pseudo-perplexity measurements, and throughput experiments.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds NeoBERT contextual document embedding results and evaluation beyond its trained context length.

M1.justification: The NeoBERT backbone, masked-language-model pre-training, and original unified fine-tuning procedure are unchanged. Section 5.2.2 and Appendix G add an application of existing CDE methodology: contextual batching, a two-backbone contextual embedding architecture, and joint training. This extends the downstream procedure without revising the core encoder.

E1.justification: GLUE, MTEB-English, and the existing training datasets remain. Appendix E adds predictive evaluation of NeoBERT4096 on Wikipedia sequences extending to approximately 7,000 tokens, beyond its trained window; v1 tested such longer lengths only for throughput. The CDE training-data description does not establish additional domain or language coverage.

E2.justification: Table 5 adds comparisons with NomicBERT/cde-v1 and ModernBERT/cde-v2 under contextual embedding fine-tuning. Appendix G.3 also adds cited leaderboard-score comparisons with GTE, BGE, and GIST. Comparator membership in the original GLUE and unified MTEB tables is unchanged.

E3.justification: V2 retains the original 2,000-step unified fine-tuning experiment but adds a substantially different CDE protocol: 235M noisy query-document pairs per epoch followed by 1.5M high-quality examples, three epochs per stage, batch and cluster sizes of 512, and contextual inputs using 512 documents. These are settings for an additional experiment, not revisions to the earlier experiment.

E4.justification: Appendix E and Figure 6 add a context-extrapolation analysis for NeoBERT4096, exposing degradation around 6,000–7,000 tokens. The original architectural ablations and sequence-length analyses remain. Appendix B.2 expands discussion of the existing tokenizer ablation without adding a new tokenizer experiment.

E5.justification: The ablation seed-control statement and throughput plus/minus reporting are retained unchanged. The added CDE results use point scores, with no new repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: New Table 5 reports CDE averages of 66.60 for NeoBERT, 65.68 for ModernBERT, and 65.00 for NomicBERT, with category scores and ranks. Figure 6 adds longer-context results. Existing GLUE, unified MTEB, and throughput scores are unchanged; 66.60 does not replace the differently configured 51.3 result. New Appendix B.2 inconsistently reports a 2.9% tokenizer drop despite Figure 1 retaining 84.0 versus 82.2, approximately 2.1%.

T1.justification: Appendix G.1 adds formal definitions of the CDE batch-clustering objective and two-backbone contextual embedding function, attributed to prior work. Existing loss and pseudo-perplexity definitions remain unchanged. No theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The conclusion additionally claims that advanced fine-tuning places NeoBERT at the top of MTEB among models under 400M parameters. This extends the earlier claim of superiority under the paper's unified fine-tuning conditions. The core architecture, efficiency, accessibility, and release claims remain.

C2.justification: Section 4 and Appendix B.2 replace the earlier tokenizer vocabulary-tradeoff hypothesis with explanations involving algorithms, training corpora, casing, and byte handling. Appendix E identifies a native extrapolation boundary near 6,000 tokens and discusses further extension requirements. Appendix G.3 adds a pre-training-data hypothesis for the CDE model's lower STS score.

D1.justification: Appendix G supplies implementation information for the added CDE experiment, including gradient caching, GTE-large for clustering and negative filtering, no cross-GPU negative sharing, and Adam with a 5e-5 learning rate, 1,000 warmup steps, and linear decay. Original pre-training hardware, GLUE hyperparameters, task instructions, and release links are unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to BGE and GISTEmbed and positions NeoBERT as a stronger backbone for CDE and a competitor to leading embedding systems. CDE itself was already cited in v1, and the main related-work section remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section order are retained. V2 subdivides the MTEB section, expands the tokenizer discussion, adds context-length and CDE appendices, and extends the conclusion. John X. Morris is added to the author list. These are localized structural and language changes.

P2.justification: V2 adds CDE Table 5 and context-extrapolation Figure 6, adds task-count headers to Table 4, clarifies Figure 1's cumulative-ablation caption, and redraws Figure 3 with revised sizing and axes. Existing appendix tables are renumbered, and Figure 5 is relocated without changing its results.

improvement.justification: The CDE comparison strengthens evidence that NeoBERT's advantages extend to advanced fine-tuning, while Figure 6 makes its context-length limitations more concrete. These additions improve empirical support beyond v1's retained experiments. However, Appendix B.2 introduces reversed tokenizer labels and a 2.9% drop inconsistent with the retained approximately 2.1% result. These localized errors temper, but do not outweigh, the added validation.
